newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia reviews BP's Piedemonte stake.
newsitem.headline: Colombia reviews BP's Piedemonte stake.

text.p: Mines and Energy Minister Rodrigo Villamizar said Thursday that the government had not yet defined terms under which British Petroleum Co Plc can operate the Piedemonte block in Colombia's oil-rich eastern plains.

Openly contradicting remarks he made to reporters Tuesday, Villamizar also said Piedemonte, which is to be exploited by BP in association with the state oil company Ecopetrol, had not yet been declared commercial.

Villamizar spoke after a high court, known as the Council of State, issued a non-binding resolution Wednesday night reversing an earlier ruling, handed down in February, that would effectively allow BP to retain a higher share of the Piedemonte profits than its contract to operate the field provides for.

The new judgment from the court, which Villamizar insisted was not legally binding, was requested by Comptroller General David Turbay, who has said planned revisions in BP's contract would cost the state up to $2.2 billion.

The Council of State's previous ruling favored BP because it supported the multinational's claim that Piedemonte's reserves were virtually all condensates and should be classified as gas rather than crude oil.
Under BP's sliding scale contract, this meant that the field's short-term profitability for BP would increase, before dropping to an eventual 30-70 percent split in favor of Ecopetrol.
The new ruling states that gas is among what are broadly defined as hydrocarbons or petroleum, so there is no reason to redefine terms of BP's association contract.

BP officials could not be reached for immediate comment. But Villamizar said that unless existing contract conditions were revised it quite was possible that the British oil giant would simply decline to exploit Piedemonte or explore it further.
Estimated reserves in the three hydrocarbon formations discovered so far in Piedemonte range anywhere between 500 million and one billion barrels of condensates.
Much of the 709,000-acre (287,000 hectare) remains unexplored, however, and it may yield much higher reserves.
Villamizar said it would now be left to the Council of Ministers, comprised by President Ernesto Samper and his 15- member cabinet, to settle the protracted contract dispute.

Despite remarks to reporters Tuesday, when he announced that Piedemonte had been declared commercial, he also said no such action had been taken so far by Ecopetrol's board of directors. Villamizar, the president of the board, offered no explanation for his erroneous announcement just two days earlier.
